nodes.title: Keep only the first visible row in state
nodes.why: The pool, the range line and the offsets all follow from one number: the row at the top edge. Storing that row rather than the pixel position means a scroll that stays inside one row sets the same value, so React skips the render; half a pixel of slack keeps a zoomed browser's 35.6px on row 1.
nodes.alternative: Store the raw scrollTop and derive the row on render.
nodes.tradeoff: The raw position is simpler to read but re-renders all twenty rows on every scroll event, about 36 times per row boundary on a slow drag.

nodes.title: Start five rows early and clamp the pool to the list

anchor.snippet: const start = Math.min(Math.max(firstVisible - OVERSCAN, 0), ITEM_COUNT - POOL_SIZE);

nodes.why: Overscan draws rows beyond the edges so a fast scroll does not show blank space before the next render. Clamping keeps twenty rows at both ends: payments 1 to 20 at the top, 9,981 to 10,000 at the bottom.
nodes.alternative: Render only the rows that intersect the viewport, ten or eleven depending on the offset.
nodes.tradeoff: Drawing only the visible rows is the least work per render, but the edges flash empty while the browser scrolls ahead of React.

nodes.title: Give the spacer the full list height
nodes.why: The scrollbar and the scroll range come from the content height. A spacer as tall as all 10,000 rows lets the reader scroll anywhere while only twenty rows exist, each translated to its own offset inside it.
nodes.alternative: Pad the list with top and bottom placeholders sized to the hidden rows.
nodes.tradeoff: Padding avoids absolute positioning, but both paddings change on every window move; one spacer and per-row offsets keep the layout fixed.

nodes.title: Follow the scroll event
nodes.why: The browser fires scroll at most once per frame, and only while the list moves, so one setState per event needs no extra throttle.
nodes.alternative: Poll scrollTop in a requestAnimationFrame loop.
nodes.tradeoff: A frame loop runs every frame even when nothing scrolls; the event costs nothing while the list is still.

nodes.title: Let a jump move the list and set the state
nodes.why: Setting scrollTop moves the list, but the scroll event it causes arrives on a later frame. Reading the position back and setting the row at once renders the new window in the same frame, from the position the browser actually applied.
nodes.alternative: Set scrollTop and let the scroll handler update the window.
nodes.tradeoff: Relying on the event is less code, but the window lags one frame behind the jump; the checks do not wait for that frame.

nodes.title: Key rows by slot to recycle their nodes
nodes.why: With a key per payment, every row that scrolls in is a new element and every row that scrolls out is destroyed. A key per slot keeps the same twenty elements: when the pool moves by one row, one element gets new text and a new offset, and React moves it to the end of the list.
nodes.alternative: Key by position in the pool (0 to 19), or keep the payment id.
nodes.tradeoff: Position keys never move a node but rewrite all twenty rows on every step; id keys are the safe default when rows hold their own state (an input, focus), because a moved slot node loses focus and carries that state to another payment.

nodes.title: Tell assistive technology the full size
nodes.why: Only twenty rows exist in the DOM. aria-setsize and aria-posinset let screen readers that support them announce a row as 1,001 of 10,000 instead of one of twenty.
nodes.alternative: Leave the list semantics to the rendered rows.
nodes.tradeoff: Support varies by screen reader, and a virtual cursor still only reaches the rendered rows; the attributes make the size honest, not the whole list browsable.
